source.title: Convergence guarantees for RMSProp and ADAM in non-convex optimization and their comparison to Nesterov acceleration on autoencoders
source.authors: A. Basu; Soham De; Anirbit Mukherjee; Enayat Ullah

record.tranche_reason: Compares adaptive optimizers with Nesterov acceleration and reports held-out performance, using different tasks and settings from the optimizer comparisons in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports training and test losses for autoencoders and training loss and test accuracy for VGG-9. It does not test random-label fitting, interpolation thresholds, batch-size generalization gaps, dropout, sharpness measures, or removing memorized examples. Figure-only values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The VGG-9/CIFAR-10 experiment tests V4 through an Adam–NAG comparison with momentum tuning and held-out classification accuracy. The autoencoder experiments measure reconstruction loss, outside V4's stated classification and language benchmarks.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the empirical findings. The authors emphasize sensitivity to both beta1 and the numerical shift parameter: high-momentum Adam often outperforms NAG on autoencoders and matches it on VGG-9/CIFAR-10. They also report RMSProp generalization failures as autoencoders grow. Their theoretical convergence guarantees do not cover the high-momentum Adam regime showing the strongest empirical performance.
record.recipe_differences: Compares ADAM and RMSProp with NAG on MNIST autoencoders and VGG-9/CIFAR-10; tunes optimizer hyperparameters and emphasizes ADAM β1 values 0.9 and 0.99. No random-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: ADAM's β1 value changes test performance; network size changes RMSProp generalization; mini-batching helps NAG on small autoencoders. The paper also reports sensitivity to ξ, with higher ξ helping test loss but potentially hurting training loss.

fits_no_version.finding: High-momentum Adam achieves lower held-out reconstruction losses than NAG on full-batch and larger mini-batch MNIST autoencoders; NAG does better on small mini-batch autoencoders.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer generalization rankings in image reconstruction depend on momentum, network size, and batching.

fits_no_version.finding: RMSProp's reconstruction generalization deteriorates as autoencoder size increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RMSProp can fail to generalize on sufficiently large MNIST autoencoders.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing the numerical shift parameter can lower Adam's test reconstruction loss while worsening training loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adam's reconstruction generalization depends on its numerical shift parameter as well as momentum.

record.problems: The reported empirical comparisons are primarily qualitative descriptions of plots, without exact test-loss or accuracy values or uncertainty estimates in the supplied text. Hyperparameter tuning was limited by computation, and selected settings were chosen by training loss at the end of 105 iterations.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately stated numeric results were available in the supplied text; plot-only values were not transcribed. The optimizer comparisons across other autoencoder sizes are summarized in R2 and R3 only where the text explicitly states the aggregate qualitative pattern.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization alongside natural-label held-out accuracy.
Test error beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classification and the role of local connectivity or initialization.

Language benchmarks; plain SGD and classical momentum comparisons; decay-schedule tuning; decoupled weight decay; switching optimizers. Broader tuning is tested only through a small momentum grid, not an extensive search.
Batch-size effects with fixed epochs and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout effects and joint dropout/weight-decay removal.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, generalization-gap ranking, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Removing examples selected by memorization influence.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V4. NAG is a relevant momentum-gradient comparator. Exact plotted values and uncertainty cannot be recovered from the supplied text. The qualitative statements suffice for the classification verdicts; autoencoder findings should remain separate from V4.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps around zero training error and test error beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the effects of local connectivity or initialization.
Language benchmarks; SGD and momentum SGD; broader optimizer tuning; decoupled weight decay and switching from Adam to SGD.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adjustments.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing examples selected by memorization influence and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: ADAM
rows.size_stated: VGG-9: 7 convolutional layers and 2 fully connected layers
rows.operation_detail: Mini-batch training on CIFAR-10; compared test accuracy at β1=0.9 and β1=0.99 with NAG.
rows.value: ADAM at β1=0.99 generalizes as well as NAG and better than ADAM at β1=0.9
rows.note: Authors describe the comparison qualitatively; exact accuracies are not stated in text.
rows.check: At beta1=0.99, the Adam disadvantage is absent: accuracy matches NAG at approximately equal training loss. Split this from beta1=0.9, where the text describes a generalization gap closed by momentum tuning; that condition has the disadvantage observed. Adam is an optimizer, and momentum tuning exceeds learning-rate-only tuning.
